headline: Salt Lake's look is a high-desert grid of salt, snow and sandstone, with a DIY print-and-mural scene that has outgrown its tourist-brochure image and a Jazz identity built on mountains and a purple note.
summary: Utah's visual culture sits between a famously orderly built environment (the numbered street grid, beehive iconography, mid-century signage) and an unusually strong outdoor-art tradition (Spiral Jetty, red rock, the Great Salt Lake's shifting pinks). The working scene is anchored by artist-run and DIY spaces around Central 9th, Sugar House and downtown, plus festivals like Craft Lake City and the Utah Arts Festival, and the West Side and Pacific Islander and Latino communities carry much of the real street-level color. For a Jazz team coming off a 22-60 season but now built around Darryn Peterson, Ace Bailey, Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr., the opportunity is a gray-and-baby-blue City Edition language that can be grounded in real Utah materials (salt, snow, shale, dusk sky) and in local makers rather than generic mountain clip art. The sharpest risk is leaning on LDS sacred imagery or flattening Pacific Islander culture into decoration.

insights.title: The grid is the graphic language
insights.detail: Salt Lake's coordinate-style addresses (a corner like 900 South and 900 East, shortened locally to 9th and 9th; 2100 South; 'the West Side') are a genuine local typography of numbers that residents use as neighborhood identity.
insights.implication: Numeric grid coordinates make a distinctive, swap-proof graphic for tees, jerseys' jock tags and hangtags in a clean sans, more ownable than another mountain silhouette.

insights.title: Salt, snow and shale beat 'generic mountain'
insights.detail: The current Jazz City Edition is a vertical gray gradient with baby blue trim, which maps naturally onto Wasatch granite, inversion haze and winter dawn, and onto the pale texture of the Bonneville Salt Flats and Great Salt Lake shoreline.
insights.implication: Build graphics from real surface textures (crusted salt, shale, snow-pack) so the gray palette reads as place, not a default colorway.

insights.title: Land art is the city's signature art world
insights.detail: Robert Smithson's Spiral Jetty (1970, Rozel Point, Great Salt Lake) and and Nancy Holt's Sun Tunnels (1976) in the Great Basin desert make Utah a land-art pilgrimage; the Great Salt Lake's low water and pink microbial color shifts are a live civic concern.
insights.implication: A spiral or shoreline-contour motif can anchor a collection, but credit and license anything derived from Smithson's work (estate/Holt-Smithson Foundation) and consider a Great Salt Lake conservation tie-in.

insights.title: Artist-run, DIY and print culture drives the scene
insights.detail: The monthly Gallery Stroll, Craft Lake City's DIY Fest, screen-print and poster shops, and the downtown and Central 9th studio clusters feed a scene of local illustrators and muralists more than a gallery-market one.
insights.implication: Commission two or three local artists via a paid, credited program for a limited graphic drop, rather than sourcing a single 'Utah' look in Portland.

insights.title: The Jazz name is a design asset with its own two eras
insights.detail: The franchise carries the 1979-96 musical-note look and the 1996-2004 purple, teal and copper mountain era, a New Orleans legacy that Utah fans treat as heritage, not baggage.
insights.implication: Nostalgic purple-and-mountain throwbacks can run alongside the gray City Edition as a heritage lane; license check on legacy marks with the team and NBA.

insights.title: Pacific Islander and Latino West Side culture is under-served visually
insights.detail: Utah has one of the largest per-capita Pacific Islander populations in the US, concentrated in West Valley City, Kearns, Rose Park and Glendale, with a visible Latino presence in Glendale and Rose Park, and the Jazz's new young core brings fresh fans from these communities.
insights.implication: Co-create with community designers, tattoo artists and church or school-based groups; never lift tatau, tapa or other ceremonial patterns without family or community permission and payment.

places.name: Utah Museum of Contemporary Art (UMOCA)
places.why: The city's main contemporary art institution and a credible partner for local artist commissions.

places.name: Utah Museum of Fine Arts (UMFA)
places.why: The state's major art museum on the U campus, useful for archive and design-history access.

places.name: Poor Yorick Studio
places.why: Independent print studio associated with the local printmaking scene; operating status and location unconfirmed.

places.name: Central 9th and 9th and 9th
places.neighborhood: 900 South, west side of downtown and 900 East
places.why: Two distinct 900 South hubs: Central 9th (around 200 West, mural and studio cluster) and 9th and 9th (around 900 East, shops and cafes); both carry the numbered-grid vernacular.

places.name: Sugar House
places.why: Neighborhood with the Sugar House Monument, small shops and murals; a fan-heavy walkable core.

places.name: Utah State Fairpark
places.why: Hosts Craft Lake City's DIY Fest, the busiest local-maker marketplace of the year.

places.name: Library Square
places.why: Home of the Utah Arts Festival each June, with architecture by Moshe Safdie that frames the city's modern look.

places.name: Spiral Jetty (Rozel Point)
places.neighborhood: Great Salt Lake north shore, Box Elder County
places.why: The state's best-known artwork and an anchor for salt-and-spiral imagery.

places.name: Delta Center
places.why: The home arena, whose surrounding downtown blocks and signage are the natural canvas for activation.

people.name: Trent Call
people.why: A widely recognized Utah-based artist whose large figurative and mural work makes him a credible collaborator for a limited graphic.

people.name: Sri Whipple
people.why: Known locally for bright murals and community-oriented work; a plausible partner for a street-level graphic.

people.name: Ben Wiemeyer
people.why: Salt Lake-based artist known for large murals and illustrated, graphic-forward work.

people.name: Robert Smithson
people.why: His work defines Utah in art history; any reference needs estate engagement, not casual borrowing.

people.name: Craft Lake City
people.role: Local nonprofit and DIY Fest organizer
people.why: Runs the main annual maker marketplace and can introduce vetted local designers and screen printers.

people.name: Salt Lake Arts Council
people.why: Runs Living Traditions and public-art programs; a route to community artists, including Pacific Islander and Latino makers.

moments.name: Gallery Stroll
moments.why: The recurring downtown opening night for galleries; an easy pop-up and artist-meet moment.

moments.name: Living Traditions Festival
moments.why: A free festival of the area's ethnic and folk arts, central for authentic Pacific Islander, Latino and other community crafts.

moments.name: Utah Arts Festival
moments.why: Library Square festival with visual artists, a likely launch moment for a collab with a local artist.

moments.name: Craft Lake City DIY Fest
moments.why: Peak local-maker visibility; the best place to find future collaborators.

moments.name: Kimball Arts Festival
moments.why: Park City's juried arts festival, drawing the affluent mountain-town audience.

moments.name: Jazz vs. Nuggets, NBA Cup group opener
moments.why: First Cup Night at home for the Jazz, an obvious early-season drop or window activation.

vocabulary.meaning: Local shorthand for the 900 South and 900 East intersection and its shop-and-cafe neighborhood; distinct from Central 9th near 200 West.
The numbered street system radiating from Temple Square, used constantly as directions and as identity.
Rose Park, Glendale and neighboring communities west of I-15, with strong Pacific Islander and Latino roots.
The winter haze that traps cold air in the valley, a shared and visual local experience.
Utah's state emblem, representing industry, seen on signs, highways and the state flag.
The state ski-tourism slogan used on license plates; it is a state-tourism phrase, so treat it as a reference, not a free slogan.
The mountain range behind the city, the dominant skyline shape.

designCues.use: Small accent for a drop graphic or lining; avoid making it dominant to protect the Jazz's identity.

designCues.source: Southern Utah canyon country, Arches and Zion
designCues.use: Warm counter-color for outdoor-oriented apparel, used sparingly.

designCues.use: Tonal print or jacquard on shorts, warm-up shells and bags.

designCues.source: Salt Lake's numbered street addresses such as 900 South and 2100 South
designCues.use: Clean sans numerals as graphic, and on jock tags and sleeve hits.

designCues.use: Tonal line graphic on a hoodie or tee; license and credit anything drawn from Smithson's work.

productHooks: A 'Grid' graphic tee and hoodie in the gray gradient with baby blue accents, built on Salt Lake coordinate addresses, with a limited run printed by a local screen shop.

A paid, credited collaboration with one or two Utah muralists or illustrators (for example Trent Call, Sri Whipple or Ben Wiemeyer, pending outreach) for a numbered release timed to the Cup opener or Gallery Stroll.
A Heritage Purple throwback capsule using the 1990s mountain-era palette, subject to license, as a counterpart to the gray City Edition.
A salt-crust and shale tonal-texture warm-up jacket and bag set, with a donation tied to Great Salt Lake conservation.
watchouts: Do not use Salt Lake Temple, temple iconography or other LDS sacred imagery or garment-related references on product.
Pacific Islander designs such as tatau, tapa and Hawaiian or Tongan ceremonial patterns require community partnership, credit and payment; never lift them.
Spiral Jetty imagery and any Smithson-derived work involve estate rights; also treat the Utah state flag, beehive emblem and tourism slogans as government IP to clear.
Legacy Jazz marks (note, purple mountain) belong to the team and NBA; coordinate all use.
